title: Brendan Eich and the Rushed Birth of JavaScript (1995)
explainer: Netscape hired Brendan Eich in 1995 expecting he'd embed the Scheme language in its browser, but management insisted the new scripting language merely look like Java — ruling out Scheme, Perl, and Python as models for its surface syntax. Eich built a working prototype in an intensely short stretch that spring, shipped first under the name LiveScript in a Navigator beta, and it was renamed JavaScript that December in a joint announcement with Sun Microsystems — a marketing move, since the language has essentially no technical relationship to Java.

title: Scheme and Self: the Languages Actually Behind this and Closures
explainer: Even though JavaScript's syntax was forced to look like Java, Eich has said directly that he modeled its closures on Scheme's first-class functions and its object system on the Self language's prototypes. That mixed ancestry is part of why JS's `this` behaves so unlike Python's explicit `self` covered elsewhere in this track — prototype-based objects were never built around a parameter-passing convention, so `this` gets assigned based on how a function is called rather than how it's defined.
